cards.title: Don't Abandon Hook Testing Because of Andromeda
cards.summary: Andromeda may group near-identical ads but rotating substantially different hooks still unlocks net-new reach for fatigued winners, so hook testing remains high-value.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep testing hooks on a fatigued winning ad or to kill it and start entirely new creative concepts.
steps: Recognize the widespread claim that Andromeda groups minor variations into single Entity IDs and therefore punishes hook testing; the source argues this leads advertisers to a mistake.
Understand that Andromeda groups visually and contextually identical ads, not every variation of a hook; the source maintains hook testing still works on live accounts.
Agree that diverse creative has always been valuable, but don't let that reasoning cancel the hook's outsized importance in paid social video.
Because the hook sells the ad, the source places roughly 90% of a creative's impact in the first 3-5 seconds, citing Ogilvy's headline logic.
Continue running hook variations on proven bodies as your default low-effort, high-ROI play rather than only producing entirely new assets.
Verify current Meta/Andromeda behavior on your own account rather than assuming the algorithm has made hook testing obsolete, because tool behavior can change.
caveats: This is the source's opinion and account experience, not a documented platform rule; confirm with your own tests.
Andromeda grouping behavior may change over time, so re-validate the assumption on live campaigns.

cards.title: Revive a Fatigued Hero Ad by Replacing Only the Hook
cards.summary: A proven testimonial ad that fatigued after months can be revitalized by attaching new 3-5 second hooks rather than discarding the asset.
cards.use_when: A previously top-performing video ad (e.g. testimonial) has fatigued after extended spend and stopped scaling.
steps: Confirm the ad is genuinely fatigued: in the source's example a top performer that ran roughly six to seven months and was about 5x better than anything else began to lose results.
Instead of filming entirely new concepts, rework only the first 3-5 seconds of the proven body.
Avoid simply repurposing more hooks from the existing footage; most of your market already saw that hook and dropped off, so reuse of the same avatar/visual rarely re-engages them.
Shoot new hooks with a different person, e.g. EGC (Employee Generated Content) delivering the hook before transitioning into the original CGC (Customer Generated Content) testimonial body.
In the source's case this restored performance to prior levels at the same daily spend, and the reworked ads became the account's current top performers.
Treat these results as one account's example, not a guaranteed outcome; test your own winner before scaling spend assumptions.
caveats: The source could not show the actual client ad, so the performance figures are uncorroborated.
Results cited (5x, six-to-seven-month fatigue, restored spend) are specific to one account and not benchmarks.

cards.title: Four Levers for Varying a Hook: Angle, Offer, Avatar, Format
cards.summary: Rotate hooks along four distinct levers—angle, offer, avatar and format—to bypass Andromeda grouping and reach genuinely new audiences.
cards.use_when: Planning hook variations for a proven ad body and choosing which dimensions to change.
steps: Lever 1 – Angle: change the messaging or contextual/seasonal framing. In the source's example the hook was made contextually relevant to the current time of year so an older-sounding testimonial felt current again.
Lever 2 – Offer: change the CTA or product focus. This often lives in the copy or headline rather than the spoken hook; e.g. pivot from a single product to a bundle or a sale.
Lever 3 – Avatar: change who delivers the hook. Using an EGC character with a very different profile from the on-screen testimonial hooks new people the original avatar missed.
Lever 4 – Format: change the first 3-4 seconds visually. Options include a 3-second static or GIF/motion-graphic intro with a written testimonial overlay that transitions into the video.
You don't need to change all four: a single lever (the source changed angle and avatar) can revitalize the ad; changing all four can also work.
Pair lever changes with volume because results depend on testing enough variations.
caveats: Combining all four levers is described as very likely to work but only 'through volume', meaning it requires producing many variations.
Changing only wording will re-hook some viewers but not everyone; a visual change is also needed for broader re-engagement.

cards.title: Test More Than Three Hooks to Beat the Odds
cards.summary: Testing only two or three hook variations per concept has low odds of producing a winner; run many variations on a proven body instead.
cards.use_when: Choosing how many hook variations to produce when revitalizing a proven winning ad.
steps: Reject the trap of limiting variations out of fear that Andromeda will group them all together; that fear can push you to under-test.

If you test only an angle change and a couple of avatar changes (the source's example of three hooks), the odds of a high performer are low unless you are an exceptional scriptwriter with deep audience knowledge.
Instead produce a higher volume of hooks on the proven body; in the source's example they ran four different hooks across two bodies, reworking both hooks and body slightly.

Budget the work so the volume is achievable: making 10 versions of a 3-5 second hook is roughly the same effort as producing one ~75-second ad body, since most shooting and editing effort lives in the body.
Because the hook drives retention, concentrate repeated low-effort iterations there while keeping the proven body intact.
caveats: The claim that 'three hooks is usually too few' is the source's heuristic, not a calculated benchmark.
The 10-versions-equal-one-body effort comparison is the source's practical estimate for their own 75-second format.

cards.title: Why Hooks Deserve the Budget: Drop-off Math
cards.summary: Most viewers drop off at the hook, so the first 3-5 seconds carry the highest ROI of the entire creative and justify disproportionate production effort.
cards.use_when: Allocating creative production time and budget between hooks versus full ad bodies.
steps: Apply the source's premise that roughly 80-90% of viewers drop off before the ad body, making the hook the most critical variable in retention.
Consequently, the source argues about 90% of advertising dollars are 'wasted' after the hook if the hook doesn't sell.
Invest most iteration effort in the first 3-5 seconds because improvements there affect the largest share of your audience.
Since producing multiple 3-5 second hooks is a fraction of the effort of full new ads, the source considers hook testing the highest-ROI creative activity.
Note the tension acknowledged by the source: an extremely good single hook could outperform, but the odds of hitting one are low, which is why volume in hooks is preferred.
Do not merely tweak scripts; combine script changes with angle, offer, avatar and format changes to reach new viewers.
caveats: The 80-90% drop-off figure and the 90% effort allocation are the source's stated premises, not independently verified benchmarks.
Treat the 'spend 90% of effort on the hook' framing as a directional principle, not a literal budget rule.

cards.title: Distinguish EGC Hooks from CGC Bodies
cards.summary: Employee Generated Content (EGC) can deliver a new hook that leads into the original Customer Generated Content (CGC) testimonial body to re-hook audiences.
cards.use_when: Structuring a testimonial ad where the hook and testimonial come from different sources to expand reach.
steps: Define EGC as Employee Generated Content, e.g. a team member or client-side person filming the opening on-camera hook.
Define CGC as Customer Generated Content, i.e. the customer providing the core testimonial that carries the ad body.
Build the ad so a new EGC hook (a different person from the original avatar) plays first, then transitions into the proven CGC testimonial.
Use a deliberately different avatar profile in the EGC hook from the one in the body to hook viewers the original presenter never reached.
Reuse the proven body unchanged underneath, since its performance is already established; only the 3-5 second intro is new.
Pair EGC hooks with angle changes when the original body's wording or visuals feel dated.
caveats: The EGC/CGC split is the source's terminology for this hybrid structure; it is not a platform-defined format.
Source's client case is one example and results are not guaranteed.

cards.title: Raise the Quality Bar for Hook Variations
cards.summary: The mechanics of hook testing haven't fundamentally changed but the quality/requirement bar to make it succeed has risen, so weak or repurposed hooks should be expected to fail.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why new hooks fail on a proven ad and deciding whether to blame the method or the execution.
steps: When new hooks fail, don't conclude that hook testing no longer works or that Andromeda killed it; first check whether you reused existing footage rather than producing genuinely different hooks.
A common failure pattern: taking hooks from the existing video and repurposing them so the majority of the market has already seen and rejected them.
The goal is to re-serve the ad to the same audience with a differently delivered hook that gets them to hold and watch through.
Recognize that a wording change alone re-hooks some viewers; add visual changes to reach those who still drop off.
Assume the bar is higher now: unless you are unusually strong at scriptwriting and audience understanding, generic variations are unlikely to hit.
Decide to increase production effort and volume (e.g. a new presenter, new context, new format intro) before concluding the approach is dead.
caveats: The claim that 'the bar has gone up' is the source's qualitative observation, not a measured threshold.
Failed hooks can be caused by poor scripts or mismatched audience, not only by algorithm changes.

input.text:
10-MCR / paid social creative and content

Goes here. Paid social creative production, hook writing, direct response video frameworks, creator/UGC scripting, static ad design, messaging strategies, evaluating stages of awareness, identifying new ad formats/angles, and creative strategist workflows.

Not here.

Paid advertising performance metrics, ROAS, scaling rules, bidding, or attribution -> 11-ADC

Google Analytics reporting or organic site analytics -> 06-MEA

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details why abandoning hook testing due to Meta's Andromeda algorithm is a mistake, outlining how to revive fatigued hero ads by varying hooks across four core levers (angle, offer, avatar, and format) to reach net-new audiences. modules: [MCR] topics: [creative strategy, hook writing, video ads] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. creative strategy / Demystifying the impact of Meta's Andromeda algorithm on creative similarity and ad delivery. Addressing the misconception that Andromeda strictly punishes minor ad variations (e.g., hook testing), explaining that while the algorithm groups visually and contextually identical ads into single Entity IDs, swapping hooks with substantial variations in avatar or format successfully bypasses this grouping and unlocks net-new reach for fatigued ads. hook writing / Establishing a high-volume hook testing framework to extend the lifespan of top-performing ad bodies (e.g., customer testimonials). Demonstrating how to rotate four core levers within a hook: Angle (the messaging/seasonal context), Offer (the call-to-action or product bundle), Avatar (the person delivering the hook, such as using Employee Generated Content to introduce Customer Generated Content), and Format (the visual presentation, such as using a 3-second static or motion graphic before transitioning to video). video ads / Revitalizing fatigued "hero" video ads (e.g., a top-performing testimonial that hits its spend threshold and stops scaling) by replacing the first 3-5 seconds rather than completely abandoning the asset. Emphasizing that since 80-90% of viewers drop off before the body of the ad, investing production effort into churning out 10+ hook variations for a single proven body yields an exponentially higher return on effort than filming entirely new concepts from scratch.

Look for. The primary misconception about Meta's Andromeda algorithm: that advertisers should stop hook testing because the algorithm will automatically group all minor variations together. The four levers to vary when testing new hooks: Angle, Offer, Avatar, and Format. The definition of EGC vs. CGC: Employee Generated Content (e.g., a team member filming the hook) versus Customer Generated Content (e.g., the customer providing the core testimonial in the ad body). The primary reason hook testing is high ROI: 80% to 90% of viewers drop off at the hook, making it the most critical variable in ad retention, and producing multiple 3-5 second hooks requires a fraction of the effort of creating entirely new ads.

Skip. General quotes from David Ogilvy unless directly tied to the mathematical value of hook testing.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume.

In the last 5 years, my team and I have helped e-commerce and retail brands generate almost half a billion dollars in attributed revenue. By the end of this video, you'll know why stop hook testing because of Andromeda is terrible advice. You'll understand exactly how Andromeda treats creative similarity and why the hook is still the highest ROI part of your entire creative system. First, I'm going to walk you through a specific example from a real account, a testimonial ad that was the best performer the account had ever seen, but it then fatigued after 6 to 7 months. Then I'm going to show you what we changed to get it performing again at the exact same daily spend, why it worked, including the caveat that most people miss. And finally, I'm going to give you a simple hook testing framework that you can go and apply to any winner that gives you the four levers to rotate through that you can apply to any winner. All right, so this is terrible advice, which is you should stop hook testing because of Andromeda. Andromeda wants diverse creative, and so now you need completely new assets every time you put a new ad in their account. I don't think this is good advice. This isn't what we're seeing performs that well on accounts at the moment. And I think that hook testing is the easiest way to take previous top performer and get it to perform well again. I'll run you through a very specific example, give you the logic, give you some data to prove it so that you don't make the mistake of stopping hook testing within your accounts. So, let's dive into it. This ad right here, a high performer on one of the accounts that we manage. Now, I can't actually show the ad because I don't have approval from the client to show it, but this is a video testimonial. Obviously, you can see that when this was launched, there were multiple bodies, two different bodies, and there were nine hooks that were tested. This was the top performing ad. This was launched back in April 27th of this year. This was by far the highest performing ad that has ever entered this ad account. It performed unbelievably well, about 5x better than anything else. Now the issue with an ad this good is all the spend goes there. This was ran for the previous six to seven months and after about six to seven months it fatigued. It was no longer getting results. And so what do you do here? Well, we could go and get other testimonials from other people. We could try to figure out another way to rework this creative. We could put it into different formats. That would be the typical advice from the Andromeda content creators. But there's a much easier solution here. In fact, there's a really easy solution. And there's a way that we got this to not only start performing again, but it's performing just as well as it ever has. And we're getting the exact same amount of daily spend throughput through it. And that is that we just went and put a bunch of new hooks on it. Now, there is a caveat here, which is that we didn't just take more hooks from the existing content and repurpose it onto the existing content. Instead, what we did is we actually shot completely new hooks of a different person. So you can think of this as EGC in the hook, employee generated content talking about the testimonial and then it goes into UGC or I guess CGC customer generated content CGC being the body. We went through recorded a bunch of different hooks with this particular client and guess what? This ad right here and this ad right here and now the current two top performers in the entire account outperforming everything else. Now, under an Andromeda friendly uh advice, people would be giving you, hey, you shouldn't be hook testing anymore. You should be thinking about completely new formats, completely new angles. You need to be going for a completely new approach. And I agree. I think that's always been the case, right? It's always good to have diverse creative, not just because Andrometer rolled out, but forever. That's always been the case. But it's also always been the case through advertising forever that that the hook is what truly matters, right? David Olgvy um a legend in copyrightiting said it follows that unless your headline sells your product you've wasted 90% of your money. So the headline aka the hook in a video is where 90% of your effort should go. And so to completely disregard hook testing in an Andromeda world because Andromeda wants diversity and it might count the bodies as the same ad and group them together. Well, I can tell you it doesn't because this is still working incredibly well in our accounts. So now how do you go and translate this into everything else? Has hook testing changed at all from 5 months ago to now? And I would say it hasn't. But the bar of quality, the bar of requirement to actually kind of make this work has gone up for sure. And so what do I mean by that? Well, the reason why most people will say this doesn't work. Hey, yeah, we we tried to put a bunch of new hooks on an ad that was working, but none of the hooks worked. This doesn't work anymore. It's because of Andromeda. Nathan's advice is wrong. The reason where they're wrong is that most people would go through this exercise that we've just gone through. But they would just take hooks from the existing video and repurpose and try to get that to work. The issue is is that majority of people in your market have probably already seen this video. They saw the hook. They didn't watch past the hook. They didn't resonate with it and therefore they moved on. And so what we're really trying to do is reserve this ad to all the people that have already seen it, but get them engaged to watch through the video through a different variation of the hook. that's going to get them to hold. And often just a change in wording can get a lot of people in, but it's not going to get everyone in. We do need a change in visuals. And there's actually four things that we can change that we should be thinking about. Number one is the angle, number two is the offer, number three is the avatar, and number four is the format. Now, in our changes of hooks, we changed the angle. We made it contextually relevant to this time of year. So, the testimonial that was being watched, it can come across outdated just based on the wording that is throughout the particular ad and the script. Therefore, we made the hook contextually relevant to this moment of the year. Number two, we changed the avatar. So, rather than the usual character being within the ad, we changed it to a piece of EGC that's actually very, very different from the avatar that's in the ad. Very different profile. And because of that, it hooks a bunch of new people that otherwise wouldn't have been hooked by the original avatar. And by changing these two things, we revitalize the ad and got it to perform well again. Now, you don't necessarily have to change the angle and the avatar. You could change the offer and the format. And we will do this as well on this ad eventually. So, what does that look like? What we're actually offering in the hook, which often you don't actually have an offer in the hook. So, this might be in the context of the copy and the headline within the meta ad. We're going to change the call to action. So where this might have been one particular product that's getting pushed, maybe we pivot into a bundle, maybe we pivot into a sale on the format. Rather than having a video hook, we can change to a static or a GIF hook. So what that looks like is a piece of like motion graphics in the back end. So it might be a 3se secondond clip of B-roll and then over the top we have a written testimonial or we have something that's going to hook people and then it transitions into the video. We could change the format to just literally be static for 3 seconds and then it moves into the video. There's so much that can be done to rework the format of the first 3 to 4 seconds. And through that, we can then hook a bunch of new people. We can get people interested that weren't interested in the initial offer. And then that obviously revitalizes the video.
